instructions: Take the 4 steaks out of the fridge and pat them dry with paper towels. If they're taller than 1 1/2 inches, press them down gently with your palm until they're about that thick. Sprinkle the heaping teaspoon of salt over them on all sides.

Put the 1 tbsp peppercorns in a zip-top bag, seal it and lay it on a cutting board. Crush them with the bottom of a heavy pan or a rolling pin until they're in coarse pieces. You want cracked, not powder.
Press the cracked pepper onto both flat sides of each steak so it sticks in an even layer.
Meanwhile, finely chop the shallot. That should be about 1/3 cup.

Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a large cast iron or stainless steel skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Lay the steaks in with space between them and leave them alone for about 4 minutes, until the underside is deep brown and they let go of the pan.

Flip them and cook the other side for about 4 minutes for medium-rare, or about 5 minutes for medium. You're cooking them to 130°F in the middle for medium-rare or 140°F for medium, so if you have a thermometer, check one there. No thermometer? Make a small cut into the center of one: medium-rare is red and juicy, medium is pink.
Transfer the steaks to a plate and cover them loosely with foil. They'll rest while you make the sauce.

Pour the extra fat out of the skillet, but don't wipe it. Leave the browned bits in. Turn the heat down to medium-low and add the 2 tbsp butter and the shallot. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring and scraping the bottom, until the shallot is soft and golden.

Take the skillet off the heat and pour in the 1/2 cup cognac. Put it back on the heat and stand back a little. It may catch fire. If it does, let the flames burn out on their own, which takes a few seconds.
Let it bubble for 2 to 3 minutes, scraping up the browned bits, until it's cooked down to a glaze that the shallot has mostly soaked up.

Stir in the 3/4 cup cream and the 1 tsp Dijon. Let it bubble gently for about 3 minutes, until it's thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Pour in any juices that have gathered on the steak plate and stir.
Taste the sauce. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Put a steak on each plate and spoon the sauce over the top.
method_notes: All three crust the steaks in coarsely crushed whole peppercorns (Billy Parisi makes the crust optional), sear them in a hot skillet, rest them, then make the sauce in the same pan by burning off cognac and simmering heavy cream until it coats a spoon. Once Upon a Chef (the lead) uses filet mignon, softens a shallot in butter before the cognac and adds a little Dijon with the cream; Alton Brown lights the cognac on purpose off the heat and uses more cream with no shallot; Billy Parisi uses strip steaks and adds garlic and thyme. This follows the lead's amounts and order. The pepper crust is the dish, so the heat stays on the steak at the lead's 1 tbsp across four steaks.
